engagement.instructions: How well does the article hold the reader's attention throughout?
criteria: Reads like filler — no tension, stakes, or reason to keep reading past the first paragraph
Informative but flat — delivers facts without making the reader care about the outcome
Holds attention — creates genuine curiosity or stakes that pull the reader through sections
Compelling — the reader would forward this to a colleague or finish it on a busy day

narrative_arc.instructions: Does the article have a clear, purposeful structure where each section builds on the last?
criteria: Random pile of facts — sections could be reordered without the reader noticing
Loosely organized — sections relate to the topic but don't build on each other
Clear progression — each section sets up the next; the reader knows where the argument is going
Satisfying arc — opens a question or tension, builds through evidence, and resolves with a concrete payoff

information_density.instructions: How well does the article back its claims with concrete facts, numbers, mechanisms, or examples?
criteria: Mostly filler — few concrete facts, numbers, mechanisms, or examples
Thin — makes claims but rarely supports them with specifics
Solid — most claims are backed by a concrete fact, number, or example
Dense and useful — nearly every paragraph teaches something specific that the reader couldn't easily guess

originality.instructions: Does the article say something the reader hasn't already read in the top search results on this topic?
criteria: Commodity content — restates what any search result already says, with no new angle
Standard take — covers the topic competently but adds no original insight, data, or framing
Has a point of view — brings a distinct angle, original observation, or proprietary data
Genuinely new — the reader learns something they haven't encountered before, backed by evidence

voice_authenticity.instructions: Does the article sound like a specific human with opinions wrote it, or like generic AI output?
criteria: Generic AI output — could have been written by any LLM with no personal input
Polished but impersonal — competent prose without any identifiable author personality
Has a voice — recognizable opinions, cadence, or personality that a different author wouldn't produce
Distinctive — the reader could guess who wrote it from the style, opinions, and lived experience

headline_delivery.instructions: Does the article deliver on the promise of its title or headline?
criteria: Bait-and-switch — the title promises something the article never addresses
Partially delivered — touches on the title's topic but leaves the main question unanswered
Delivered — the reader gets what the title promised, though nothing extra
Overdelivered — answers the title's promise and gives the reader more than they expected

opening_strength.instructions: Does the opening earn the reader's next 30 seconds?
criteria: Generic opener — could apply to any article on any topic ("In today's world…")
Topical but slow — names the subject but doesn't create a reason to keep reading
Direct and grounded — opens with a concrete fact, claim, or observation that sets up the article
Hooks immediately — the first 2–3 sentences create tension, surprise, or a question the reader needs answered

closing_strength.instructions: Does the ending leave the reader with something concrete to remember or act on?
criteria: Trails off or summarizes — restates the article or ends with vague platitudes
Wraps up but adds nothing — ends cleanly without leaving the reader with a new thought or action
Concrete takeaway — ends on a specific decision rule, next action, or insight
Sticks — the ending reframes the topic or gives the reader something they'll remember and act on
